etymologies.etymologyHTML: Inherited from Middle English hole, hol, from Old English hol (“orifice, hollow place, cavity”), from Proto-West Germanic *hol, from Proto-Germanic *hulą (“hollow space, cavity”), noun derivative of Proto-Germanic *hulaz (“hollow”), which is of uncertain ultimate origin. Related to hollow.

definitions.definition: A hollow place or cavity; an excavation; a pit; a dent; a depression; a fissure.

quote.citation: c. 1606–1607 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Anthonie and Cleopatra”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene vii]:
quote.text: To be called into a huge sphere, and not to be seen to move in't, are the holes where eyes should be, which pitifully disaster the cheeks.

quote.citation: 1879, R[ichard] J[efferies], chapter II, in The Amateur Poacher, London: Smith, Elder, & Co., […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Orion hit a rabbit once; but though sore wounded it got to the bury, and, struggling in, the arrow caught the side of the hole and was drawn out. Indeed, a nail filed sharp is not of much avail as an arrowhead; you must have it barbed, and that was a little beyond our skill.

definitions.definition: An opening that goes all the way through a solid body, a fabric, etc.; a perforation; a rent.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, 2 Kings 12:9:
quote.text: The priest took a chest, and bored a hole in the lid.
[…] her palfrey’s footfall shot Light horrors thro’ her pulses: the blind walls Were full of chinks and holes; and overhead Fantastic gables, crowding, stared: […]

definitions.definition: (golf) A subsurface standard-size hole, also called cup, hitting the ball into which is the object of play. Each hole, of which there are usually eighteen as the standard on a full course, is located on a prepared surface, called the green, of a particular type grass.
(golf) The part of a game in which a player attempts to hit the ball into one of the holes.
(baseball) The rear portion of the defensive team between the shortstop and the third baseman.
(chess) A square on the board, with some positional significance, that a player does not, and cannot in the future, control with a friendly pawn.
(stud poker) A card (also called a hole card) dealt face down thus unknown to all but its holder; the status in which such a card is.
In the game of fives, part of the floor of the court between the step and the pepperbox.
(heading) In games.
(archaeology, slang) An excavation pit or trench.
(figuratively) A weakness; a flaw or ambiguity.

quote.text: But between the drinks and subtle things / The holes in my apologies, you know / I’m trying hard to take it back

definitions.definition: (Can we verify(+) this sense?) (informal) A container or receptacle.
(physics) In semiconductors, a lack of an electron in an occupied band behaving like a positively charged particle.
(computing) A security vulnerability in software which can be taken advantage of by an exploit.
(slang, derogatory) A person's mouth.
(slang) Any bodily orifice, in particular the anus.
(Ireland, Scotland, vulgar) A vagina.
(informal, with "the") Solitary confinement, a high-security prison cell often used as punishment.

quote.citation: 1988 April 2, Ed Mead, “AIDS hysteria sweeps prison guards' union”, in Gay Community News, page 9:
quote.text: In late December a Washington State prisoner was involved in a scuffle with a guard who was trying to take him into the hole.

quote.citation: 2011, Ahmariah Jackson, IAtomic Seven, Locked Up but Not Locked Down:
quote.text: Disciplinary actions can range from a mere write up to serious time in the hole.

definitions.definition: (slang) An undesirable place to live or visit.

quote.citation: 1887, Harriet W. Daly, Digging, Squatting, and Pioneering Life in the Northern Territory of South Australia, page 109:
quote.text: I have often heard people say, "One can't live upon a view," and I have heard some of the most beautiful places called "awful holes," simply because of the monotonous lives led in them.

definitions.definition: (figurative) Difficulty, in particular, debt.
(graph theory) A chordless cycle in a graph.
(slang, rail transport) A passing loop; a siding provided for trains traveling in opposite directions on a single-track line to pass each other.
(Canada, US, historical) A mountain valley.
(transitive) To make holes in (an object or surface).
(transitive, by extension) To destroy.
(intransitive) To go into a hole.

quote.citation: 1631, Ben Jonson, The Staple of News, act IV, scene ii:
quote.text: Good master Picklock, with your worming brain, And wriggling engine-head of maintenance, Which I shall see you hole with very shortly! A fine round head, when those two lugs are off, To trundle through a pillory!

definitions.definition: (transitive) To drive into a hole, as an animal, or a billiard ball or golf ball.

quote.text: If the player holes the red ball, he scores three, and upon holing his adversary's ball, he gains two; and thus it frequently happens, that seven are got upon a single stroke, by caramboling and holing both balls.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To cut, dig, or bore a hole or holes in.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: hole (comparative holer or more hole, superlative holest or most hole)

definitions.definition: Obsolete spelling of whole.

quote.citation: 1843,  Sir George Webbe Dasent (translator), A grammar of the Icelandic or Old Norse tongue (originally by Rasmus Christian Rask)
quote.text: Such was the arrangement of the alphabet over the hole North.

definitions.definition: Misspelling of whole.
